opus-5.5.text:
I think this is probably the central question for the field right now. Language models had this enormous gift: decades of people writing things down on the Internet, for their own reasons, and that text just happened to be the right format for training. Robotics doesn't have that. Nobody has been uploading joint torques and gripper states for twenty years. So we have to think much more deliberately about where the data comes from.

The way I see it, there are a few layers. The most direct one is teleoperation: people physically controlling robots to collect demonstrations. That gives you the highest-quality data, perfectly matched to the robot, but it's expensive and it scales roughly linearly with human hours. Even large efforts pooling data across many labs are still tiny compared to Internet text. So teleoperation alone won't get us there, though it remains important as the "gold standard" anchor.

The second layer, which a lot of my group's work focuses on, is learning from humans doing things naturally. Humans already perform an enormous amount of manipulation every day. If we can capture that with lightweight, wearable devices—egocentric cameras, smart glasses, hand tracking—then data collection becomes a byproduct of people living their lives, rather than a dedicated labor process. That starts to look more like the Internet: data generated passively, at scale. The hard research problem is the embodiment gap—human hands aren't robot grippers, and our bodies move differently—so you need models and representations that can transfer across that gap.

The third layer is simulation and generative models. Simulation gives you nearly unlimited interaction, and increasingly we can use generative models to create diverse scenes, objects, and even plausible trajectories. But there's always the question of realism, especially for contact-rich physical interaction, so I see simulation as an amplifier rather than a replacement for real-world data.

And then there's the existing Internet video, which already contains lots of people manipulating objects. It lacks action labels, but it carries a lot of information about how the world works and what tasks look like, so it's useful for pretraining world understanding.

So I don't think there will be a single "Internet for robotics." It'll be a data pyramid: a broad base of passive, cheap, weakly labeled data—videos and human activity—then a middle layer of structured human data and simulation, and a small top layer of high-quality robot data to ground everything in the actual body. The infrastructure challenge is not just collecting more; it's building the tools, standards, and learning algorithms that let all these heterogeneous sources talk to each other. That's what I think will ultimately unlock scaling for robot foundation models.

r001.rationale: The response calls data infrastructure central and says it will unlock scaling, but does not frame it as decisive for how long robot-model research can continue.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is honestly the central question in robot learning right now, and I want to be careful about the analogy, because it's both the right framing and a bit of a trap.

The right part is obvious. Language models worked because there was a decade or two of humans writing things down for their own reasons, and that text happened to be the perfect training signal. Nobody built the Internet to train GPT. It was a byproduct of billions of people doing something useful to them. Robotics has nothing like that. There is no natural byproduct of human life that looks like a robot's observation-action stream. Nobody is going around logging joint torques and camera frames while they load a dishwasher.

So the trap is assuming we just need to "collect the Internet for robots" by brute force, mostly through teleoperation. I've been part of efforts like that, and I think they're valuable, but if you look at the numbers, we're talking about tens of thousands of hours of demonstrations, and the Internet is on the order of trillions of tokens. The gap is many orders of magnitude, and teleoperation scales linearly with human time. It doesn't get cheaper the way text did.

My view is that the data problem has to be attacked from a few directions at once. One is leveraging what already exists. Human video is the closest thing we have to a natural large-scale source of information about how the physical world works and how bodies interact with objects. The embodiment gap is real, but a lot of what a robot needs, which is roughly what objects afford, how tasks decompose, what the sequence of a manipulation looks like, is in that data. The second is simulation, where the question is less about photorealism and more about generating diverse tasks and scenes cheaply enough that the long tail gets covered. And the third, which I think is underrated, is making the robots themselves the data engine. Once you have a policy that works even moderately well, deployment generates data at a rate no teleoperation lab can match. The challenge is making that data useful rather than just large, which means thinking hard about how you get supervision out of autonomous rollouts, how you handle failures, and how you keep the distribution from collapsing.

The other thing I'd push on is that the Internet gave language models more than scale. It gave them diversity for free. Every topic, every style, every weird corner of human activity. Robot datasets today are extremely narrow by comparison, often a handful of tasks in a handful of labs. I actually think diversity is the more important axis to optimize than raw hours, and it's the one that's harder to get by just hiring more operators.

So to directly answer your question: I don't think we'll get a single artifact that plays the role the Internet played. I think we'll get a composite, with human video and simulation providing breadth, teleoperation providing high-quality anchors, and robot deployment providing scale over time. The infrastructure work is in making those sources compatible with each other, so a model can actually learn from all of them jointly. That's a less glamorous answer than "we need a billion demonstrations," but I think it's the honest one.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls data infrastructure “the central question in robot learning right now,” but does not say it will determine how long the robot-model research agenda can continue.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s one of the central challenges in robotics. For language models, the Internet already contained a huge amount of text that people had created for other purposes. In robotics, we don’t have an equivalent collection of robots taking actions and observing what happens.

And the key is that we need more than images or videos. A video can show you someone picking up a cup, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you what forces they applied, what the robot should do when the cup slips, or how a particular action changes the world. That interaction data is much harder to collect.

So I think the infrastructure has to combine several sources. We can learn a lot from human video, collect demonstrations on robots, and use simulation to explore situations that would be expensive to reproduce physically. But we also need a loop where robots attempt tasks, we identify where they fail, and those failures guide the next round of data collection.

The question is really how to make that loop scale. Can collecting useful data become part of operating a robot, rather than a separate experiment every time? And can experience collected on one robot help another robot with a different body? If we can do that reliably, then we start to have something that plays a similar role to the Internet—even though it will probably look very different.

r001.rationale: The response calls data infrastructure a central challenge and asks how the data loop can scale, but it does not say that infrastructure determines how long the robot-model research agenda can continue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how to build a data ecosystem where experience can accumulate across robots, tasks, and environments. For language models, the Internet provided this enormous collection of human-generated data. In robotics, we don’t have an equivalent resource that captures what an agent did, what happened as a result, and whether it succeeded.

So part of the challenge is collecting more data, but another part is making that data useful across different systems. If one robot learns something in one environment, how much of that experience can help another robot with a different body or a different set of sensors? We need infrastructure that preserves enough context to support that transfer, and ways to evaluate whether adding data actually improves the model.

I also think this has to be a loop. You collect experience, train a model, deploy it, and use its failures to decide what data to collect next. The equivalent of the Internet for robotics may look less like a static repository and more like a system that keeps generating useful experience as robots interact with the world.

r001.rationale: The response calls building a robotics data ecosystem a key question and describes its challenges, but it does not say that data infrastructure determines how long the robot-model research agenda can continue.
